title: Epistolae
author: Sidonius Apollinaris
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0261.stoa0002.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: non nequiter te concilii tempore post sedentes censentesque iuvenes inglorium rusticum, senem stantem latitabundum pauperis honorati sententia premat, cum eos quos esset indignum si vestigia nostra sequerentur videris dolens antecessisse? sed quid plura? si pateris hortantem, conatuum tuorum socius adiutor, praevius particeps ero, sin autem inlecebrosis deliciarum cassibus involutus mavis, ut aiunt, Epicuri dogmatibus copulari, qui iactura virtutis admissa summum bonum sola corporis voluptate determinat, testor ecce maiores, testor posteros nostros huic me noxae non esse confinem. vale.
passages.english: Is it not a wretched thing that at the time of council young men, sitting after you and giving their opinions, should crush you, an inglorious rustic, and that as an old man standing and skulking you should be crushed by the vote of a poor man who has held office, when you see with grief that those whom it would be unworthy [even] to follow in our footsteps have gone ahead of you? But why say more? If you put up with my urging, I will be the ally and helper of your efforts, your forerunner and partner; but if, entangled in the alluring nets of pleasures, you prefer, as they say, to be joined to the doctrines of Epicurus, who, accepting the loss of virtue, defines the highest good as the pleasure of the body alone, see, I call our ancestors to witness, I call our descendants to witness, that I am no neighbour to this fault. Farewell.
passages.notes: The opening sentence is syntactically difficult; 'pauperis honorati sententia premat' is rendered as the vote of a poor man who has held office. The construction of 'senem stantem latitabundum' (whether it describes the addressee or someone else) is uncertain.

passages.original: pariter et, prout singulis cordi, diversa censentes sermocinabamur, cur a quibusdam protomystarum tamquam scaevus cavendusque tractator improbaretur, quamquam sic esset ad verbum sententiamque translatus ut nec Apuleius Phaedonem sic Platonis neque Tullius Ctesiphontem sic Demosthenis in usum regulamque Romani sermonis exscripserint. studiis hisce dum nostrum singuli quique, prout libuerat, occupabantur, ecce et ab archimagiro adventans, qui tempus instare curandi corpora moneret, quem quidem nuntium per spatia clepsydrae horarum incrementa servantem probabat competenter ingressum quinta digrediens, prandebamus breviter copiose, senatorium 1 ad morem, quo insitum institutumque multas epulas paucis parabsidibus apponi, quamvis convivium per edulia nunc assa nunc iurulenta varietur, inter bibendum narratiunculae, quarum cognitu hilararemur institueremur, quia eas bifariam orditas laetitia peritiaque comitabantur, quid multa?
passages.english: At the same time, holding different opinions as each one pleased, we were discussing why he was rejected by certain of the chief priests as a perverse author to be guarded against, although he had been translated so [faithfully] word for word and in sense that neither Apuleius transcribed Plato's Phaedo, nor Tully Demosthenes' Ctesiphon, so well into the usage and rule of the Roman language. While each one of us was occupied with these pursuits as he pleased, behold, someone came from the chief cook to warn that the time was at hand for refreshing our bodies; and indeed the water-clock, which keeps the increase of the hours through its measured spaces, showed that this messenger had entered at the right time, as the fifth [hour] was passing. We lunched briefly [but] plentifully, in the senatorial manner, by which it is ingrained and established custom that many foods are served on few dishes, although the meal is varied with dishes now roasted, now stewed. While drinking [there were] little stories, by learning which we might be amused and instructed, since, being composed in two ways, they were accompanied by mirth and learning. Why say more?
passages.notes: 'He' refers to Origen (from the preceding context), translated by Rufinus. 'Ctesiphontem' refers to Demosthenes' speech On the Crown, delivered in defence of Ctesiphon. 'senatorium 1': the 1 is a footnote mark, omitted. The syntax of the water-clock clause ('probabat ... quinta digrediens') is compressed and the reading uncertain.

passages.original: ad extremum nemo saeculo meo quae voluit affirmare sic valuit, si- quidem dum sese adversus eum, quem contra loquitur, exertat, morum ac studiorum linguae utriusque symbolam iure sibi vindicat, sentit ut Pythagoras dividit ut Socrates, explicat ut Platon implicat ut Aristoteles, ut Aeschines blanditur ut Demosthenes irascitur, vernat ut Hortensius aestuat ut Cathegus, incitat ut Curio moratur ut Fabius, simulat ut Crassus dissimulat ut Caesar, suadet ut Cato dissuadet ut Appius persuadet ut Tullius. iam si ad sacrosanctos patres pro comparatione veniatur instruit ut Hieronymus destruit ut Lactantius adstruit ut Augustinus, attollitur ut Hilarius summittitur ut Iohannes, ut Basilius corripit ut Gregorius consolatur, ut Orosius affluit ut Rufinus stringitur, ut Eusebius narrat ut Eucherius sollicitat, ut Paulinus provocat ut Ambrosius - perseverat. iam vero de hymno tuo si percontere quid sentiam, commaticus est copiosus, dulcis elatus, et quoslibet lyricos dithyrambos amoenitate poetica et historica veritate supereminet, idque tuum in illo peculiare, quod servatis metrorum pedibus pedum syllabis syllabarumque naturis intra spatii sui terminum verba ditia versus pauper includit nec artati carminis brevitas longitudinem phalerati sermonis eliminat;
passages.english: In short, no one in my age has had such power to establish what he wished to; for when he exerts himself against the man he is speaking against, he rightly claims for himself a share in the manners and studies of both languages: he perceives like Pythagoras, divides like Socrates, unfolds like Plato, entangles like Aristotle, coaxes like Aeschines, rages like Demosthenes, blooms like Hortensius, seethes like Cethegus, urges on like Curio, delays like Fabius, feigns like Crassus, dissembles like Caesar, advises like Cato, advises against like Appius, persuades like Tullius. Now if one comes to the most holy fathers for comparison, he instructs like Jerome, demolishes like Lactantius, builds up like Augustine, rises high like Hilary, comes down low like John, rebukes like Basil, consoles like Gregory, flows abundantly like Orosius, is concise like Rufinus, narrates like Eusebius, appeals like Eucherius, challenges like Paulinus, perseveres like Ambrose. Now if you ask what I think of your hymn, it is concise yet copious, sweet yet lofty, and it surpasses any lyric dithyrambs whatever in poetic charm and historical truth; and this is peculiarly yours in it, that, while the feet of the metres, the syllables of the feet, and the natures of the syllables are preserved, the poor verse encloses rich words within the bounds of its space, and the brevity of the constricted poem does not shut out the length of adorned speech;
passages.notes: Sentence division follows the sense of the paired comparisons; in the patristic series the punctuation of the edition (commas before 'ut Basilius', 'ut Orosius', etc., and the dash before 'perseverat') is ambiguous, and pairings could be read differently (e.g. 'rebukes like Basil, consoles like Gregory' vs. the edition's grouping). 'Cathegus' taken as Cethegus. 'Symbolam' = share/contribution. 'Iohannes' presumably John Chrysostom or John Cassian; 'Gregorius' probably Gregory of Nazianzus. 'Commaticus' = composed in short clauses, here rendered 'concise'.

passages.original: debent igitur vel aequaevi vel posteri nostri universatim ferventibus votis alterum te ut Demosthenen, alterum ut Tullium nunc statuis, si liceat, consecrare, nunc imaginibus, qui te docente formati institutique iam sinu in medio sic gentis invictae, quod tamen alienae, natalium 1 vetustorum signa retinebunt: nam iam remotis gradibus dignitatum, per quas solebat ultimo a quoque summus quisque discerni, solum erit posthac nobilitatis indicium litteras nosse.
passages.english: Therefore our contemporaries and descendants ought, all together and with fervent prayers, to consecrate you, as a second Demosthenes and a second Tully, now with statues, if it were allowed, now with portraits: [they] who, formed and instructed by your teaching, even now in the very bosom of an unconquered people, though a foreign one, will keep the marks of their ancient birth. For now that the grades of rank have been removed, by which the highest used to be distinguished from the lowest, henceforth the only mark of nobility will be to know letters.
passages.notes: 'natalium 1': the 1 is a footnote mark, omitted. 'sic' in 'sinu in medio sic gentis' is awkward and possibly corrupt; it is left untranslated.

passages.original: Varronem logistoricum, sicut poposceras, et Eusebium chronographum misi, quorum si ad te lima pervenerit, si quid inter excubiales curas, utpote in castris, saltim sortito vacabis, poteris, postquam arma deterseris, ori quoque tuo loquendi robiginem summovere.
passages.english: I have sent Varro's Logistoricus, as you had asked, and Eusebius' Chronicle. If their polish reaches you, and if amid your cares of watch-keeping, as is natural in camp, you have at least some chance leisure, you will be able, after you have cleaned your weapons, to remove the rust of speaking from your mouth too.
passages.notes: 'lima' (file, polish) may refer to the quality or finish of the copies; the sense is uncertain.

passages.original: Cum primum Burdigalam veni, litteras mihi tabellarius tuus obtulit plenas nectaris florum margaritarum, quibus silentium meum culpas et aliquos versuum meorum versibus poscis, qui tibi solent per musicum palati concavum tinnientes voce variata quasi tibiis multiforatilibus effundi, sed hoc tu munificentia regia satis abutens iam securus post munera facis, quia forsitan satiricum illud de satirico non recordaris: Satur est cum dicit Horatius euhoe.
passages.english: As soon as I came to Bordeaux, your letter-carrier handed me a letter full of nectar, flowers and pearls, in which you blame my silence and ask for some of my verses in return for your verses, which are usually poured out for you, ringing through the musical hollow of the palate with varied voice, as if from many-holed pipes. But you do this, fully enjoying royal generosity, now carefree after receiving gifts, because perhaps you do not remember that satirical remark about the satirist: 'Horace is well fed when he cries euhoe.'
passages.notes: The final quotation is from Juvenal on Horace. 'euhoe' is the Bacchic cry.
